newsitem.title: UK: Gold Outlook - Eyes $350 but miners may set ambush.
newsitem.headline: Gold Outlook - Eyes $350 but miners may set ambush.

text.p: The gold market realised its potential to rally this week after the price broke through the $345 per ounce resistance barrier last Friday, dealers said.
Bullion fixed at $348.20 on Monday, its highest level for a month, continuing a rally which began with a sharp fall in the dollar against the yen late last week.
Bulls are now eyeing the prospect of $350-$360 to pave the way for further gains. But analysts say miners are likely to be preparing to ambush the market anywhere beyond $350.
"I believe we have seen the bottom for the year and I think it's starting to turn," said Rhona O'Connell, metals markets analyst at T.Hoare and Co.

She forecast a ride towards $350-$352, adding that gold's flat performance over the past month in the $337.50-$343 range had frustrated the shorts, who were expecting further dips to at least finance the cost of rolling those positions forward.
Added to this was a strong price elastic response from physical buyers below $340, which helped lift the bearish influence of the prospect of central banks activating their gold reserves.
"At the start of the year the shorts had the upper hand," O'Connell said. "We had the specs successfully driving it lower, then the physical demand coming in as a help to cushion it."
But the situation took a new twist as some professionals decided to lock in profits and close their short positions.

"I understand from dealers that it's very very difficult to get hold of 99.99 (high purity) metal at the moment, which suggests that the Far East in particular is sucking it up like a vacuum cleaner," O'Connell said.
But while the sudden rise had polished up the charts, analysts remained unable to make a bullish case for gold.
"It's extremely difficult to see what could put prices up as high as $355-$360. Certainly jewellery demand is unlikely to do it," said Ted Arnold, metals analyst at Merrill Lynch.
More and more producers were looking to be forward sellers on good rallies, particularly if the U.S. Federal Reserve raised interest rates again this month.
The chances of that happening were slimmer, though still possible, after recent tame U.S. economic data.
Gold players will comb through fresh data this week, including U.S. retail sales for April on Tuesday, producer prices on Wednesday and industrial production on Thursday.
Susan Rigg of Chart Analysis said a hike towards the peak in March of $364.95 could be on the cards.
"But we may have to do some more work before we see a sustained rise," she said.
Steep rises for platinum and palladium continued on Monday amid protracted delays in Russian supplies.
Platinum fixed at $395.25 against Friday's $383.50, its highest since February 28, and palladium was up $7.25 at $171.75, its highst since April 20, 1995.
The world's biggest palladium exporter and second biggest platinum exporter has been absent from the market since December after difficulties arose in renewing contracts for leading buyer Japan.
Analysts said once Russia resumed its exports, prices would ease, but not to any dramatic extent.
"It is possible that huge amount of fund interest in the market these days will keep palladium prices in the $150-$155 an ounce area," said Arnold.
